The Labrador is an exceptionally popular dog. As of 2006, it was widely considered one of the most popular dog breeds, and it is the most popular dog by ownership in Canada, New Zealand[[45]](#cite_note-46) and the United Kingdom.[[46]](#cite_note-47) In 2006, in both the United Kingdom and the United States, there were well over twice as many registered Labradors as the next most popular breed.[[47]](#cite_note-uk_kc_stats-48)[[48]](#cite_note-akc_stats-49) If the comparison is limited to dog breeds of a similar size, then there are around 3–5 times as many Labradors registered in both countries as the next most popular breeds, the [German Shepherd](/wiki/German_Shepherd "German Shepherd") and the Golden Retriever.[[47]](#cite_note-uk_kc_stats-48)[[48]](#cite_note-akc_stats-49)

Labs are the most popular breed of [assistance dog](/wiki/Assistance_dog "Assistance dog") in the United States, Australia and many other countries,[[49]](#cite_note-Alecia-50) as well as being widely used by police and other official bodies for their detection and working abilities. Approximately 60–70% of all guide dogs in the United States are Labradors.

In 2022 Labrador Retrievers were the second-most-popular breed in the United States.[[50]](#cite_note-51) In 2020 the Labrador was the most popular registered dog breed in New Zealand.[[51]](#cite_note-52)

Seven out of the thirteen "outstanding [gundogs](/wiki/Gundog "Gundog")" of the [Australian National Kennel Council](/wiki/Australian_National_Kennel_Council "Australian National Kennel Council")'s 2000–05 appointees to its 'hall of fame' are Labradors.[[52]](#cite_note-53)

The Central League's [Nishi Nippon Pirates](/wiki/Nishi_Nippon_Pirates "Nishi Nippon Pirates") existed for one season—they placed sixth in 1950, and the following season merged with the [Nishitetsu Clippers](/wiki/Nishitetsu_Clippers "Nishitetsu Clippers") (also based in Fukuoka) to form the [Nishitetsu Lions](/wiki/Nishitetsu_Lions "Nishitetsu Lions"). This brought the number of Central League teams down to an ungainly arrangement of seven. In 1952, it was decided that any Central League team ending the season with a winning percentage below .300 would be disbanded or merged with other teams. The [Shochiku Robins](/wiki/Shochiku_Robins "Shochiku Robins") fell into this category, and were merged with the [Taiyō Whales](/wiki/Taiy%C5%8D_Whales "Taiyō Whales") to become the [Taiyō Shochiku Robins](/wiki/Taiy%C5%8D_Shochiku_Robins "Taiyō Shochiku Robins") in January 1953. This enabled the Central League to shrink to an even number of six teams.

In 1954 a new [Pacific League](/wiki/Pacific_League "Pacific League") team was founded, the [Takahashi Unions](/wiki/Takahashi_Unions "Takahashi Unions"), to increase the number of teams in that division to eight. Although the team was stocked with players from the other Pacific League teams, the Unions struggled from the outset and finished in the second division every season. In 1957, the Unions were merged with the [Daiei Stars](/wiki/Daiei_Stars "Daiei Stars") to form the [Daiei Unions](/wiki/Daiei_Unions "Daiei Unions") (and again bringing the number of Pacific League teams down to seven). The Unions existed for a single season, finishing in last place, 43-1/2 games out of first. In 1958, the Unions merged with the [Mainichi Orions](/wiki/Mainichi_Orions "Mainichi Orions") to form the [Daimai Orions](/wiki/Daimai_Orions "Daimai Orions"). This enabled the Pacific League to contract from the ungainly seven-team arrangement to six teams.

After these various franchise developments, by the end of the 1950s, Nippon Professional Baseball had contracted from the initial allotment of 15 teams down to the current number of 12.

The London School of Economics and Political Science was founded in 1895[[13]](#cite_note-LSEHistoryAbout-13) by [Beatrice](/wiki/Beatrice_Webb "Beatrice Webb") and [Sidney Webb](/wiki/Sidney_Webb,_1st_Baron_Passfield "Sidney Webb, 1st Baron Passfield"), [Graham Wallas](/wiki/Graham_Wallas "Graham Wallas") and [George Bernard Shaw](/wiki/George_Bernard_Shaw "George Bernard Shaw")[[14]](#cite_note-LSEHistoryWebbs-14) initially funded by a bequest of £20,000[[15]](#cite_note-SpartacusLSE-15)[[16]](#cite_note-Statisticians-16) from the [estate](/wiki/Estate_(law) "Estate (law)") of Henry Hunt Hutchinson. Hutchinson, a lawyer[[15]](#cite_note-SpartacusLSE-15) and member of the [Fabian Society](/wiki/Fabian_Society "Fabian Society"),[[17]](#cite_note-SmithLSEandEducation-17)[[18]](#cite_note-LSEPassfieldArchives-18) left the money in trust, to be put "towards advancing its [The Fabian Society's] objects in any way they [the [trustees](/wiki/Trustee "Trustee")] deem advisable".[[18]](#cite_note-LSEPassfieldArchives-18) The five trustees were Sidney Webb, [Edward Pease](/wiki/Edward_R._Pease "Edward R. Pease"), Constance Hutchinson, [W. S. de Mattos](/wiki/W._S._de_Mattos "W. S. de Mattos") and William Clark.[[15]](#cite_note-SpartacusLSE-15)

LSE records that the proposal to establish the school was conceived during a breakfast meeting on 4 August 1894, between the Webbs, Louis Flood, and [George Bernard Shaw](/wiki/George_Bernard_Shaw "George Bernard Shaw").[[13]](#cite_note-LSEHistoryAbout-13) The proposal was accepted by the trustees in February 1895[[18]](#cite_note-LSEPassfieldArchives-18) and LSE held its first classes in October of that year, in rooms at 9 John Street, [Adelphi](/wiki/Adelphi,_London "Adelphi, London"),[[19]](#cite_note-LSEHistory1895-19) in the [City of Westminster](/wiki/City_of_Westminster "City of Westminster").
